archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (process over results)
archetype.definition: A team whose 5-on-5 chance and possession shares sit around league average or better, but whose goaltending, penalty kill and finishing have buried it at the bottom of the standings in the opening weeks.

report.headline: Shot share says middling team; goaltending and penalty kill say 0-3-2.
report.take:
The Kings are winless through five games, and the site has them 31st of 32. They have 11 goals for and 21 against, a differential of -10, and only two standings points from a pair of overtime losses. Nothing in the record suggests a team that can play. The underlying numbers tell a different story. At 5-on-5 Los Angeles has a 50.7% share of expected goals (16th) and a 53% share of shot attempts (10th). That is a team holding its own at even strength. It is not a team getting caved in.

The damage is concentrated in two places. Darcy Kuemper has started four of the five games with an .847 save percentage and -5.3 goals saved above expected. The team's goalies sit at -8.1 GSAx, 30th in the league. The penalty kill has stopped 57.9% of chances, 31st. Together they produce a PDO of 93.5, far below the 100 average, the profile of a team on the wrong end of the bounces. Panarin, Kempe and Byfield are all above 60% in expected-goals share yet carry -5, -3 and -5 ratings. That gap comes from the goals going in behind them, not from how they are playing.

The early numbers do hide one real problem: this team doesn't score enough, and that isn't new. Last season Los Angeles ranked 29th in offense, and only a +5.6 in points beyond its goal differential kept a 35-27-20 season afloat. It is 29th again now. It managed one goal in each of its last three games, against Florida, Vegas and Edmonton. The bottom six also gets outchanced: Haula (35.9%), Moore (38.3%) and Laughton (42.4%) are all well under water in expected-goals share. On the blue line, Drew Doughty's 39% in 20-plus minutes a night is a concern on a unit graded F. Brandt Clarke, at 74.1% with four points, is carrying the defensive group almost by himself.

The goaltending is the piece most likely to turn. Two seasons ago this franchise led with defense, ranking 2nd in goals against with +10.9 GSAx, and a sub-.850 save percentage rarely survives a full season. If the saves normalize and the kill climbs toward its usual range, the losses become a mediocre team's losses rather than a bottom-three team's. The scoring ceiling still caps how far this climbs, and a five-game hole in a competitive Pacific leaves little room. Expect a bubble team that will spend months making up for October.

strengths.title: Holding play at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Even with the losses piling up, Los Angeles is controlling more than half the shot attempts and splitting expected goals. It has done this against Colorado, Florida, Vegas and Edmonton, a demanding opening slate. The shot-share profile matches the last two seasons, so it looks like the team's real identity rather than a five-game fluke.

strengths.title: Top line driving play
strengths.body: Panarin, Kempe and Byfield each log about 21 minutes a night and win their minutes clearly on chances. Panarin leads the forwards with three goals and 16 shots. Their negative plus-minus is a goaltending artifact. If the saves come, this trio should start converting its territorial edge into wins.

strengths.title: Brandt Clarke breaking out
strengths.body: Clarke is the one defenseman playing like a top-pair piece. He leads the blue line in points and shots, takes power-play time, and posts a 74.1% expected-goals share. He ranks 35th on the defensemen tab while every other Kings regular sits outside the top 170.

concerns.title: Goaltending in free fall
concerns.body: Kuemper's .847 save percentage and -5.3 GSAx in four starts are the single biggest reason for the record. The team-wide -8.1 GSAx ranks 30th. Some of it should regress, since this organization posted +10.9 GSAx two seasons ago. Until it does, the margin for error is gone.

concerns.title: Penalty kill is leaking
concerns.body: A 57.9% kill ranks 31st and turns every penalty into a coin flip. Last season's kill was already soft at 74.6%, so it won't fully correct itself. The current level is still extreme enough that bad goaltending is surely part of it.

concerns.title: Scoring is a structural problem
concerns.body: The offense ranks 29th for the second straight year, the power play converts 15.8%, and the last three games produced one goal apiece. The bottom six is being outchanced badly, so goals beyond the top line are scarce. Unlike the goaltending, nothing in the numbers says this fixes itself.

trend.note: Goals against settled after the 8-4 opener in Colorado, with October allowing 3.25 a game. The offense then dried up to 1.75 a game, and the losing streak sits at five.

weekAhead.headline: Three hot goaltending teams test an offense already stalled
weekAhead.body:
Boston comes to Los Angeles as the site's 5th-ranked team, with A grades across forwards, blue line and goaltending, the 3rd-best defense and a team PDO of 107.6. The Kings then fly east for Washington and the Islanders. Both are .500 clubs, but their goalies rank 3rd and 4th in GSAx. For a team scoring 2.2 a game, three straight opponents getting strong goaltending is the worst possible matchup.

There are openings. Washington's power play converts only 13.3%, so the Kings' leaky kill is less exposed there. Boston's kill (76%) is beatable. The Islanders give up points to defensemen, which suits Clarke. Escaping the week with a win or two would count as a reset. Another goaltending collapse against these teams could make the hole very deep.

keyMatchups.title: Kings top line vs Boston wingers
keyMatchups.body: Boston holds opposing wingers furthest under expectation of almost anyone, 3rd in the league. That is exactly where Panarin and Kempe do their damage. Boston's 107.6 PDO suggests some of its success is hot shooting and saves, but at home this is still the toughest game of the week.

keyMatchups.title: Cold shooters vs hot goalies
keyMatchups.body: Washington (+6.1) and the Islanders (+5.6) both get well-above-expected goaltending. The Islanders' unit carries an A grade. The Kings' shot-share edge will need volume, because one-goal nights won't beat those netminders.

keyMatchups.title: Clarke against the Islanders
keyMatchups.body: New York ranks 22nd in points allowed to defensemen, and defensemen take a larger share of points against it than league norm. Clarke's puck-moving and power-play role make him the Kings' best bet to exploit it.

weekAhead.watch: Kuemper's save percentage. If it climbs toward normal, the Kings' even-strength play is good enough to steal games; if not, the streak extends.

restOfSeason.body:
The goaltending and the PDO are the numbers most likely to move. A team splitting expected goals with this roster shouldn't keep a sub-94 PDO or an .847 starter for long, and the 2024-25 club showed this core can defend at an elite level. Expect goals against to fall meaningfully and the record to track closer to a roughly .500 points pace. The penalty kill should improve but probably stays below average, as it was last year.

What doesn't regress is the offense. Two straight seasons near the bottom in goals, a weak power play and an outchanced bottom six cap the upside. Last year's points total was also padded by close-game luck the team can't count on again. Starting 0-3-2 in a division where Edmonton, Vegas and Seattle are off fast, the Kings look like a bubble team fighting uphill for a wild card.
swingFactors: Whether Kuemper's save percentage recovers or the crease changes hands
Secondary scoring beyond the Panarin-Kempe-Byfield group
Penalty kill climbing out of the bottom two

confidence.note: Five games; save and PDO numbers this extreme are mostly noise at this sample.
